catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alb:
Alb, a white linen vestment, has close-fitting sleeves falling nearly to the ground, secured by a girdle, or cincture. In the past it bore many names. Linea or tunica linea comes from its material. Poderis, tunica talaris, or simply talaris comes from reaching to the feet. Camisia comes from its shirt-like nature. Alba comes from its white colour, and alba Romana contrasts with shorter tunics favoured outside Rome. Of these, alba almost alone survives.

Medieval writers also use alb, plural albae, for the white garments newly baptized persons assumed on Holy Saturday. They wore them until Low Sunday, consequently known as dominica in albis, the Sunday of laying aside the white garments. Low Sunday and Trinity Sunday, with preceding days, seem sometimes to have been called Albae.
doe-osti-3014247-multi-entity-simulation:
Trevor Hardy, Mitch Pelton, Nathan Gray, and co-authors at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote this December 2025 report on multi-entity simulation with the CoSim Toolbox. Modern grid studies couple many simulators at once: power flow, buildings, markets, and communications, each running its own clock. Co-simulation tooling wires them together, and the toolbox described here manages that wiring for analysis teams.

A central database ships inside the toolbox's Docker container and launches with it, holding scenario configuration and shared metadata in one place. Model wrapper classes query the database automatically, so each simulator picks up the same configuration instead of relying on hand-passed files. The authors argue this removes a common source of error: team members unknowingly running different versions of the same scenario.
